newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South African Nobel laureates clash over truth.
newsitem.headline: South African Nobel laureates clash over truth.

text.p: Nobel peace laureate Desmond Tutu, at loggerheads with former South African president F.W. de Klerk over the truth behind apartheid crimes, said on Friday he had helped secure the Nobel prize for de Klerk.

Tutu was responding to a decision by de Klerk's opposition National Party to temporarily boycott the Truth and Reconciliation Commission because of an emotional attack the archbishop made on de Klerk on Thursday.

"The shocking statement by Archbishop Tutu...indicating that (he has) already found the National Party and F.W. de Klerk guilty of all atrocities committed during the apartheid era is a travesty of what was intended by the commission process," a party statement said.
Tutu, who chairs the commission, disclosed for the first time that he backed de Klerk behind the scenes for the Nobel peace prize he was jointly awarded with President Nelson Mandela in 1993.

Addressing a news conference, he said: "When the Nobel peace prize committee were going to award the prize, the chairman of the committee telephoned me and asked me: 'We want to give the award to Mr Mandela and Mr de Klerk, what do you think?'...

"If I had an animus against Afrikaners or against Mr de Klerk, I would have said: 'Not on your life'. But I said: 'It should be wonderful for the process of healing our country'," said Tutu, who won the peace prize in 1984.

He rejected de Klerk's accusations that the commission, which heard testimony from both the National Party and Mandela's ruling African National Congress (ANC) this week, had treated the ANC with kid gloves.
Tutu said he had once threatened to quit as commission chairman because the ANC appeared to be on the brink of giving itself amnesty for its actions during the apartheid war.

The ANC, which told a news conference in Johannesburg it was "horrified" at the NP pullout, lashed out at de Klerk, saying his emotional apology for apartheid was an insult since he denied white governments authorised apartheid crimes.

"Mr de Klerk went there claiming to be ignorant (of apartheid crimes).... But he went there knowing in great detail...what happened in...the ANC camps which were outside the country," ANC acting secretary-general Cheryl Carolus said.
"Yet he claims he didn't know what happend at Vlakplaas (the notorius police hit squad), which was under his direct jurisdiction and in his backyard."

National Party spokesman Jan Bosman told reporters the party planned to go to court to force the commission to act within the parameters of legislation which set it up, and which specified that the commission should not show political bias.
A member of the commission, Wynand Malan, said on Friday the reconciliation process was in crisis, but Tutu dismissed this. He said it had become routine for people to use him as a whipping boy.
Tutu told a news conference on Thursday that testimony to the commission on Wednesday by de Klerk, the last white president, was unacceptable.
Tutu said he had nearly broken down in tears when de Klerk maintained that torture and murder were never government policy during the apartheid years.
